issues.text: Whether the Government's preliminary objections concerning admissibility, including ratione temporis, ratione loci, manifestly ill-founded nature, and lack of victim status, should be dismissed

anchor.surface_text: The respondent Government in their submissions on the merits challenged the admissibility of the application relying on the following grounds: (1) inadmissibility ratione temporis and (2) ratione loci; (3) the manifestly ill‑founded nature of the application; and (4) the applicant's lack of locus standi.

issues.text: Whether the Government's preliminary objection concerning non-exhaustion of domestic remedies raised after the admissibility decision can be taken into account at this stage

anchor.surface_text: the Government raised an additional preliminary objection concerning non-exhaustion of domestic remedies in the light of the “Law on Compensation for Immovable Properties Located within the Boundaries of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” adopted on 30 June 2003.

issues.text: Whether there has been an unjustified interference with the applicant's right to respect for his home in violation of Article 8 of the Convention

anchor.surface_text: The applicant in his application complained of an unjustified interference with the right to respect for his home in violation of Article 8 of the Convention. The relevant provision reads as follows:

issues.text: Whether Turkey can be held liable under the Convention for acts of the authorities of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus

anchor.surface_text: The respondent Government reiterated that Turkey could not be held liable under the Convention for the acts of the authorities of the “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” (“TRNC”).

issues.text: Whether the applicant's claims under Article 8 should be considered in the context of the political situation in Cyprus and the de facto state of affairs on the island

anchor.surface_text: They further maintained that the applicant's claims needed to be considered in the context of the political situation in Cyprus and the de facto state of affairs on the island.

issues.text: Whether the notion of “home” in Article 8 of the Convention covers a property where one no longer lives but has roots

anchor.surface_text: In addition, they contended that the notion of “home” in Article 8 of the Convention could not be interpreted to “cover an area of the State where one has grown up and where the family has its roots but where one no longer lives” (Loizidou v. Turkey (merits), op. cit., § 66).

issues.text: Whether the applicant's home was under the control of the Turkish armed forces and whether this constitutes a continuous and unjustified interference with his right to respect for his family life and home

anchor.surface_text: he maintained that his continuous inability to access and use his home as well as that fact that the house and his personal effects were used by the Turkish armed forces, constituted a continuous and unjustified interference with his right to respect for his family life and his home.

issues.text: Whether the complete denial of the right of the applicant to respect for his home constitutes a continuing violation of Article 8 of the Convention

anchor.surface_text: Accordingly, it concludes that there has been a continuing violation of Article 8 of the Convention by reason of the complete denial of the right of the applicant to respect for his home.

issues.text: Whether the continuous denial of access to the applicant's property and loss of control constitutes a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1

anchor.surface_text: Accordingly, it concludes that there has been and continues to be a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention by virtue of the fact that the applicant is denied access to and control, use and enjoyment of his property as well as any compensation for the interference with his property rights.

issues.text: Whether the acts of the TRNC authorities can be justified as control of use of property by the general interest under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1

anchor.surface_text: the Government pleaded that, even assuming an issue could arise under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the control of the use of property by the “TRNC” authorities was justified by the general interest.

issues.text: Whether the applicant has an effective remedy in respect of the alleged violations, in breach of Article 13 of the Convention

anchor.surface_text: The applicant complained of lack of an effective remedy in breach of Article 13 of the Convention, which reads as follows:

issues.text: Whether the Court should have re-examined the case in light of the new Law on Compensation for Immovable Properties in the TRNC and the Government's letter raising a preliminary objection of non-exhaustion of domestic remedies

anchor.surface_text: In my opinion, before delivering its judgment in the present case, the Court should have examined the new situation in the light of the new legislation and at least requested observations from the respondent Government, particularly bearing in mind that the latter were presumably unaware that delivery of the judgment was imminent.

issues.text: Whether the Court's refusal to reopen admissibility or reconsider preliminary objections after new legislation constitutes an erroneous interpretation of the Convention

anchor.surface_text: The Court held that, following the decision on the admissibility of the application, the preliminary objection of failure to exhaust domestic remedies could no longer be raised (see paragraph 20 of the judgment). That, to my mind, is an erroneous interpretation of the relevant provisions of the Convention.

issues.text: Whether the Court's strict and rigid application of time-limits for lodging observations on admissibility issues failed to take into account the political and legal context of the case

anchor.surface_text: It is regrettable that in a case as sensitive and unusual as the present one the Court should have failed to take into account the political and legal context, instead taking refuge in a strict and rigid application of the time-limits for lodging observations on the issue of admissibility.

holdings.text: Dismisses by six votes to one the Government's preliminary objections
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court rejected the Government's preliminary objections including ratione temporis, ratione loci, manifestly ill-founded nature, and lack of victim status, relying on prior case law and procedural rules.

holdings.text: Holds by six votes to one that there has been a violation of Article 8 of the Convention
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found a continuing violation of Article 8 due to the complete denial of the applicant's right to respect for his home, applying prior case law and interpreting 'home' broadly.

holdings.text: Holds by six votes to one that there has been a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court concluded there has been and continues to be a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 by denial of access and control of property, following prior judgments and rejecting Government justifications.

holdings.text: Holds unanimously that it is not necessary to examine the applicant's complaint under Article 13 of the Convention
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found no pleadings on the Article 13 complaint and thus deemed it unnecessary to examine the complaint under Article 13.

holdings.text: Holds six votes to one that the respondent State is to pay the applicant, within three months from the date on which the judgment on the merits becomes final according to Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, EUR 2,875 (two thousand eight hundred and seventy five euros) in respect of costs and expenses plus any tax that may be chargeable, to be converted into Cypriot pounds at the rate applicable on the date of settlement; that from the expiry of the above-mentioned three months until settlement simple interest shall be payable at a rate equal to the marginal lending rate of the European Central Bank during the default period plus three percentage points
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court awarded costs and expenses claimed by the applicant as reasonable and necessary, with interest at ECB marginal lending rate plus three percentage points.

holdings.text: Holds unanimously that the question of the application of Article 41 is not ready for decision in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage; accordingly, reserves the said question in that respect; invites the Government and the applicant to notify the Court of any agreement that they may reach; reserves the further procedure and delegates to the President of the Chamber the power to fix the same if need be
holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court reserved the question of just satisfaction under Article 41 for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage as the matter was not ready for decision, allowing for possible agreement between parties.

outcome.relief_summary: Violation of Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 found; preliminary objections dismissed; Article 13 complaint not examined; costs and expenses awarded to applicant; question of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage reserved for later decision.
directions: Respondent State to pay applicant EUR 2,875 in respect of costs and expenses within three months of final judgment.
Simple interest payable from expiry of three months until settlement at ECB marginal lending rate plus three percentage points.
Question of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage reserved for future determination.
Government and applicant invited to notify Court of any agreement reached.
Further procedure reserved and delegated to President of the Chamber to fix if necessary.
